case_study_insert.main_stem: Clearspire Filtration (CSF) is a partnership in the industrial filtration sector, producing pleated air and coolant filter cartridges for manufacturing plants, employing a workforce of 34. Founded in 2013 by Sofia Almeida and Rafael Duarte, the partnership operates a flat structure with shared democratic decision-making and is based in Joinville, Brazil. CSF plans to invest $780,000 in a new automated pleating and welding line, financed by hire purchase of $480,000 on the machinery and a $300,000 overdraft facility. It has fixed costs of $312,000 a year, a variable cost of $18.00 a unit and a selling price of $30.00, and currently produces 48,000 units a year. CSF faces a serious quality problem: the defect rate on pleated cartridges has risen to 3.4%, driving 12 complaints this quarter.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log and Market Research Summary — Q3 2025: The pleating line produced 11,500 units last quarter at a defect rate of 3.4%, up from 2.0% a year ago, driving 12 customer complaints. Average order fulfilment is 4.1 days. Market research of 210 plant managers found that 74% would pay up to 5% more for filters guaranteed to reach 99% filtration efficiency and 61% want same-day quotation turnaround. Under the new Quality Assurance plan, in-process checks will replace most Quality Control final inspection, with sampling covering 1 in 20 cartridges. Off-the-job courses at the local technical institute cost $600 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Clearspire Filtration as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.00%, the third rise this year, increasing repayment costs on variable-rate business loans and hire purchase. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.1% from $14.10 to $15.10 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills across manufacturing. (3) Polypropylene media and aluminium frame costs have risen 13.2% year-on-year, industrial inflation is running at 8.3%, and manufacturing output grew 1.9% in the same period.

questions.question_text: CSF plans to finance its pleating-line expansion partly with hire purchase. Explain two advantages for CSF of using hire purchase instead of the overdraft facility.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the $480,000 machinery cost over fixed instalments matched to the productive life of the new pleating and welding line, so CSF keeps more short-term cash available for wages and materials while the 12 current complaints are cleared. Fixed instalments are also easier to budget than an overdraft, whose interest rate can move with every base-rate rise and whose full balance can be demanded at any time.

Point 2: Under hire purchase the machinery secures itself — CSF gains use of a productive asset immediately with ownership passing on the final payment — whereas an overdraft is unsecured short-term debt best suited to working-capital gaps, not a $780,000 expansion. Using hire purchase for the line preserves the $300,000 overdraft as a flexible buffer for seasonal demand and unexpected repairs, rather than being fully absorbed by the purchase and leaving the partnership with no liquidity headroom. Fixed instalments also make month-by-month cash planning far more reliable for a two-partner business without a specialist finance team.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Clearspire Filtration and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: CSF is launching its guaranteed 99% filtration efficiency cartridge range. Consider a stand at a national HVAC trade fair, a switch to online search advertising, or a direct mail and email campaign to plant managers. Which should CSF choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
HVAC trade fair stand: A fair concentrates plant engineers, maintenance contractors and filter distributors in one venue, ideal for demonstrating guaranteed 99% efficiency cartridges and booking on-site trials. The drawbacks are heavy stand, travel and logistics costs before the new line has even proved itself, a short two-day window of impact, and the risk that major national accounts attend only selectively.

Online search advertising: Pay-per-click ads capture plant managers actively searching for replacement filters and same-day quotes — exactly the 61% who want same-day quotation turnaround — with granular budgets, measurable cost per enquiry and instant coverage across Brazil. Its limits are wastage on irrelevant searches, the need for continuous budget because visibility stops when spend stops, and difficulty conveying the tactile quality of a cartridge without strong landing pages and proof downloads.

Direct mail and email campaign: A targeted mailing to the 210 plant managers CSF researched, supported by technical datasheets, can communicate efficiency data and the 5% premium story with a personalised same-day quotation reply path. It is inexpensive and trackable via reply codes, but response rates are typically low, purchased lists may be stale, and reaching brand-new buyers beyond the known list is impossible without reinforcement.

Recommendation: CSF should choose online search advertising. It captures the 61% wanting same-day turnaround at the exact moment of need, fits a small flat partnership's budget better than a trade fair, and scales nationally without the waste of a mailing to cold names. The trade fair is rejected as high fixed cost before capacity is proven; direct mail is rejected as too low-yield for a launch and too dependent on the researched 210 contacts; online advertising should be paired with a short follow-up call sheet so enquiries convert into on-site trials with the new 99% efficiency guarantee.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of CSF with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of CSF with a well-justified recommendation explaining why the trade fair stand and direct mail are rejected.

questions.question_text: CSF operates a flat structure with shared democratic decision-making. Explain two benefits for CSF of using democratic leadership to improve motivation among its filter-line staff.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 34 employees a genuine voice in how the new pleating and welding line is staffed, which satisfies their esteem needs (Maslow) and aligns with the partnership's shared decision-making culture. Staff who help set welding speeds and sampling plans are more likely to own the 3.4% defect problem, suggest process fixes and show up consistently — vital while 12 complaints are outstanding and only 4.1 days separate order from delivery.

Point 2: Participation surfaces tacit knowledge from the people who handle pleated cartridges every hour — for example which polypropylene media batches crease badly and which welding settings hold seams tightest. Acting on those insights improves quality, reduces the waste behind final inspection, and raises commitment, lowering the risk of losing scarce pleating-line skills while the $780,000 investment beds in, all without the payroll strain of hiring additional supervisors in a flat partnership. Because both partners still work the line daily, this democratic input costs nothing extra — ideas surface through ordinary shift huddles rather than new committees.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to CSF's leadership culture, quality problem, complaints and expansion.

questions.question_text: CSF needs a supervisor for the new pleating line. Consider recruiting internally from its existing 34 staff or recruiting externally. Which should CSF choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Internal recruitment: Promoting a proven pleating or welding operator who already lives the flat, democratic culture rewards loyalty, costs almost nothing in advertising or agency fees, fills the role quickly, and gives that employee a visible career step that can lift morale across the small team. The person also arrives with working knowledge of CSF's media batches, seam tolerances and complaint history — gold during commissioning of a $780,000 line. The risks are resentment from non-promoted colleagues, a skills gap left on the shop floor, and no fresh perspective on the new automation.

External recruitment: An external supervisor could bring commissioning experience from a larger filter or HVAC manufacturer, objective eyes on the 3.4% defect rate, and authority to challenge drifting habits. However, the local market for pleating specialists is thin, agency fees and notice periods are real money for a small partnership, cultural fit with shared democratic decision-making is uncertain, and external starters typically need three to six months to learn CSF's exact tolerances — during which complaints could rise further.

Decision: CSF should recruit internally, promoting the strongest pleating-line mentor and pairing them with a short off-the-job supervision course at the local technical institute ($600 per employee). This is fast, cheap and culturally safe while the new line beds in and the 3.4% defect rate must be crushed quickly; hiring externally is rejected for now because of cost, fit risk and slow ramp-up. If, after commissioning, the new line needs capabilities CSF genuinely lacks — for example welding automation diagnostics — CSF should run a focused external search rather than compromise the flat culture that keeps its 34 staff engaged.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of internal and external recruitment with limited application to CSF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the advantages and disadvantages of one or both recruitment routes in the context of CSF.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both recruitment routes in the context of CSF with a well-justified decision covering cost, culture, capability and supervision for the new line.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how CSF's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $30.00 − $18.00 = $12.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $12.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Calculate CSF's average total cost per unit.
sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Average total cost = (Fixed costs ÷ Output) + Variable cost per unit. Substitution: ($312,000 ÷ 48,000) + $18.00 = $6.50 + $18.00 = $24.50. Answer: average total cost is $24.50 per unit.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways CSF's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 26,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 48,000 units to confirm the line is comfortably profitable, with a margin of safety of 22,000 units, informing whether to accept the new 99% efficiency orders without overstretching the two partners.
2. Contribution per unit of $12.00 lets CSF model the 5% premium the 74% of plant managers will pay, raising the price to $31.50 if efficiency is guaranteed, letting managers judge whether extra quality assurance spend is justified by the higher margin.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $312,000 and contribution per unit helps managers test whether cash flow can service the hire purchase instalments of $480,000 and the potential $300,000 overdraft before committing to further press capacity.
4. Managers can use average total cost of $24.50 a unit to benchmark each quarter, pinpoint waste behind the 3.4% defect rate and 12 complaints, and judge whether the Quality Assurance sampling plan of 1 in 20 cartridges is catching defects before they leave the Joinville works.

questions.model_answer: (i) Contribution per unit = $12.00 | (ii) average total cost = $24.50 per unit | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 22,000 units against 48,000-unit output; pricing the 5% premium at $31.50; servicing the $480,000 hire purchase and $300,000 overdraft; and average-total-cost benchmarking at $24.50 to attack the 3.4% defect rate.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate CSF's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has CSF's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.40 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.50 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.95 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.05 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $90,000 inventories + $145,000 trade receivables + $45,000 cash = $280,000; 2025 current assets = $100,000 + $165,000 + $65,000 = $330,000. 2024 = $280,000 ÷ $200,000 = 1.40; 2025 = $330,000 ÷ $220,000 = 1.50. Quick cover 2024 = ($280,000 − $90,000) ÷ $200,000 = $190,000 ÷ $200,000 = 0.95; 2025 = ($330,000 − $100,000) ÷ $220,000 = $230,000 ÷ $220,000 = 1.05.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened sensibly. Short-term cover improved from 1.40 to 1.50 and quick cover from 0.95 to 1.05, meaning CSF no longer has to sell its pleated cartridges to pay short-term debts — important while hire purchase instalments on the $480,000 machinery and reliance on a $300,000 overdraft both tighten monthly cash commitments. Cash rose from $45,000 to $65,000 and inventories only edged up $10,000, showing tight stock control. The warning sign is trade receivables rising from $145,000 to $165,000: if plant managers stretch payment terms, quick cover could slide back below 1.0, and the partnership's modest capital base (capital employed of $1,700,000 against non-current assets of $1,550,000) leaves limited room for comfort.

Conclusion: CSF's financial position has improved. Short-term cover (1.40 to 1.50) and quick cover (0.95 to 1.05) show stronger short-term solvency, and the improvement does not depend on inventory build-up. The main residual risk is the $20,000 rise in receivables layered on a relatively small capital base, so CSF should tighten credit terms for new filter accounts and reserve part of the overdraft for commissioning contingencies rather than day-to-day trading.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables, cash and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether CSF's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for CSF of shifting from Quality Control final inspection to Quality Assurance built into the pleating line.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Quality Assurance prevents defects at source rather than catching them at the end, which directly attacks the 3.4% defect rate and the 12 complaints recorded this quarter. With in-process checks on each stage — checking 1 in 20 cartridges as planned — CSF can prove consistent efficiency to the 74% of plant managers demanding guaranteed 99% filtration, win the 5% premium, and cut the scrap and rework that currently consumes margin on 11,500 units a quarter.

Disadvantage: Building Quality Assurance into the pleating and welding process requires upfront investment in gauges, staff training and revised sampling routines — real money for a partnership already stretching to hire purchase of $480,000 and an overdraft facility. If the in-process checks slow cycle time or flag false rejects, unit output falls and the 4.1-day fulfilment promise slips; and if monitoring lapses once the new line is running steadily, inspection discipline fades, letting defects reach customers who were promised a guarantee rather than a hope.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to CSF's quality data, research, costs and fulfilment record.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.00%, the 7.1% minimum wage increase and the 13.2% rise in input costs will affect CSF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.00%): The 0.75 percentage point rise lifts the cost of CSF's variable-rate exposures: hire purchase of $480,000 would add 0.75% × $480,000 = $3,600 a year if variable, and a fully drawn $300,000 overdraft would add 0.75% × $300,000 = $2,250 a year — an illustrative $5,850 a year altogether. That is significant against fixed costs of $312,000, and higher base rates also make any future borrowing for expansion costlier, though the new line is already largely secured through hire purchase rather than an unsecured loan.

Minimum wage increase (7.1%, to $15.10 per hour from April 2026): CSF's 34 staff are mostly hourly press and packing operatives, so the rise is unavoidable. The insert gives no hours worked or pay split, so no annual wage total can be invented; the honest benchmark is productivity: 48,000 units ÷ 34 staff ≈ 1,412 units per worker a year. If productivity holds, the rise is absorbable; if pleating-line disruption during commissioning lowers output per worker, unit labour cost climbs and the $12.00 contribution per unit erodes quickly.

Input cost inflation (13.2% polypropylene media and aluminium frames): CSF's $18.00 variable cost is dominated by media and frames, though the insert never decomposes it, so only an illustrative bound is defensible: if the whole variable cost rose 13.2% it would add 13.2% × $18.00 = $2.38 per unit (0.132 × $18.00 = $2.376); at 48,000 units a year that is about $114,048 (0.132 × $18.00 × 48,000). Even a gentler illustrative $1.50 per unit would strip about $72,000 a year. Recovery depends on holding the 5% premium the 74% of managers will pay — now roughly $1.50 per unit at $30.00 — so the margin gain from quality may be consumed entirely by input inflation.

Conclusion: The 13.2% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds on every unit of the 48,000 CSF sells, can wipe out in one swoop the entire $12.00 contribution gain from the 99% efficiency guarantee programme, and cannot be fixed by choosing a different finance product. The minimum wage rise is second, significant but manageable through productivity near 1,412 units per worker if commissioning goes smoothly; the interest rate rise is third, at an illustrative $5,850 a year. CSF should lock supplier contracts now, push the 5% premium hard with guaranteed-efficiency customers, and keep the overdraft for contingencies only.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to CSF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on CSF's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of CSF with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
